common_name: J.C. van Tol English Holly (Self-Fertile Spineless English Holly)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; J.C. van Tol is a long-cultivated English holly selection valued for setting a heavy berry crop without a separate male pollinator nearby.

directions: J.C. van Tol is one of the oldest and most widely planted English holly cultivars, prized because a single plant reliably sets a heavy crop of bright red winter berries without a separate male pollinator growing nearby, unlike most dioecious English holly selections. Its smooth-edged, nearly spineless dark green leaves make it noticeably more pleasant to handle and prune than sharply spined straight-species holly, while still forming a dense, upright evergreen screen or specimen. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and give it partial shade to full sun for the heaviest berry set. Shear lightly in late winter if a more formal hedge shape is wanted, since the plant tolerates pruning well and recovers quickly.

common_name: Argentea Marginata English Holly (Silver-Margined Variegated English Holly)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; a female cultivar, Argentea Marginata needs a male English holly such as 'J.C. van Tol' or 'Blue Prince' within pollinating range for a heavy berry set.

directions: Argentea Marginata is a classic variegated English holly cultivar, its spiny dark green leaves edged in a broad, creamy-white to silvery margin that brightens shaded plantings year-round far more than the plain green species. As a female selection, it produces abundant bright red berries in fall and winter when a male English holly cultivar is planted within pollinator range, and the berry display reads especially vividly against the pale-edged foliage. It grows into a large, dense, pyramidal shrub or small tree over time and tolerates shearing well if kept as a clipped hedge or topiary form rather than left to its natural size. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and watch for reversion shoots of solid green foliage, which should be pruned out to preserve the variegation.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic, moist, loamy soil in full sun to partial shade; Filicoides is a slow-growing, irregular hinoki cypress selection best sited where its unusual fern-like foliage sprays can be seen up close.

directions: Filicoides is an old, distinctive hinoki cypress cultivar named for its dense clusters of thick, cord-like, dark green branchlets that radiate outward like the fronds of a fern, a strikingly different texture from the flattened, fan-shaped sprays of the straight species. Growth is slow and irregularly upright, with an open, sculptural, somewhat gnarled habit that develops real character with age and makes it a favorite accent or specimen conifer in Japanese-style gardens. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic, loamy soil, and give it full sun to partial shade, since hinoki cypress does not tolerate drought or waterlogged, alkaline conditions. Established plants need only occasional pruning to remove dead interior growth and to control size in smaller gardens.

common_name: Nanko Ume (Nankou Japanese Apricot, Premier Umeboshi Cultivar)
subcategory: East Asian ornamental-edible stone fruit tree

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Nanko is the classic large-fruited Japanese apricot cultivar grown around Minabe in Wakayama Prefecture, the traditional heartland of Japanese ume production, and benefits from a second Prunus mume cultivar nearby for reliable cross-pollination.

directions: Nanko is the most widely grown fruiting Japanese apricot cultivar in Japan, prized around its home region of Minabe in Wakayama Prefecture for large, thin-skinned, richly flavored fruit that yields an exceptionally high percentage of flesh to pit, the standard by which other umeboshi-grade ume cultivars are judged. Like other Prunus mume selections it flowers in late winter to early spring on bare branches, opening pale pink, fragrant blossoms well before leaf-out, followed by green-yellow fruit that ripens to gold through late spring into early summer. Because Nanko is only partially self-fruitful, plant a second Japanese apricot cultivar nearby to ensure a heavy crop for salt-pickling into umeboshi or steeping in shochu for umeshu. Prune to an open vase shape after fruiting to maintain airflow and fruiting wood, and harvest fruit while still firm and green-yellow for traditional pickling, or let it fully ripen to gold for fresh eating or liqueur.
sources: Wakayama Prefecture agricultural extension ume cultivar records
general horticultural reference on Prunus mume cultivars

common_name: Safari Sunset Leucadendron (Dark Red Cut-Foliage Conebush)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in sharply drained, lean, phosphorus-poor, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Safari Sunset is the best-known Leucadendron salignum hybrid cultivar, grown worldwide for the cut-foliage trade. Never use standard fertilizer, which is toxic to proteas at normal phosphorus levels.

directions: Safari Sunset is the most commercially important Leucadendron cultivar in the international cut-foliage trade, bred in South Africa and valued for its bold, deep crimson to burgundy-red bracts that intensify through the cool months and hold their color for weeks after cutting, both fresh and dried. The plant itself is a dense, upright, male-flowering shrub with narrow, leathery gray-green leaves that recede visually behind the colorful bract clusters at the branch tips. Like other Leucadendron salignum selections, it demands sharply drained, lean, low-phosphorus soil in full sun; standard garden fertilizers containing normal phosphate levels can quickly kill it, so use a protea-formulated low-phosphorus feed or none at all. Cut stems for arrangements throughout the cool season, and shape the plant lightly after the main color display fades to keep growth dense and floriferous.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Protea Family Cut Flower Production
South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI) PlantZAfrica

common_name: Savoy Express Cabbage (Early Compact Crinkle-Leaf Savoy Cabbage)

planting.note: Start transplants 4-6 weeks before setting out; set out 8-12 weeks before first fall frost for the classic autumn crop, or 3-4 weeks before last spring frost for an earlier spring crop, since Savoy Express matures notably faster than most savoy cultivars.

directions: Savoy Express is a fast-maturing, compact savoy cabbage bred to bring the deeply crinkled, tender-leaved character of savoy types to gardeners in far less time than standard savoy cultivars, forming smallish, round, moderately dense heads in about two months from transplant. Its early maturity and small footprint make it a good fit for succession planting, small raised beds, and gardeners in short-season climates who still want the delicate, sweet flavor and tender texture savoy cabbage is prized for. Like other savoy types it tolerates hard frost well and improves in sweetness after cold exposure, though its quick maturity also lets it beat summer heat in a spring planting where standard cabbages would bolt or turn bitter. Start seed indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and rotate with non-brassica crops on a three-year cycle to prevent clubroot buildup.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Savoy Express cabbage variety notes
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Cabbage Variety Trials

common_name: Zabeliana Cherry Laurel (Low Spreading Dwarf Cherry Laurel)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs or root semi-hardwood cuttings in late summer to fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Zabeliana is a low, wide-spreading cherry laurel cultivar suited to banks, foundation plantings, and mass groundcover use rather than a tall hedge.

directions: Zabeliana is a low, wide-spreading cherry laurel cultivar that grows several times wider than it is tall, forming a dense mat of narrow, willow-like, glossy dark green leaves distinctly finer-textured than the broad leaves of standard cherry laurel. Small, fragrant white flower spikes appear in mid-spring, followed by cherry-like fruit that ripens from red to black, though the plant is grown primarily for its foliage and spreading habit rather than for bloom or fruit. Like other cherry laurel selections it tolerates the deep, dry shade cast by mature trees better than almost any other broadleaf evergreen, making it a dependable groundcover-scale shrub for shaded banks, slopes, and foundation plantings where a tall hedge is not wanted. Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and prune lightly only to control spread, since Zabeliana needs little maintenance once established. All plant parts other than ripe fruit pulp are toxic if ingested.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

common_name: Lime Magic Acacia (Chartreuse-Foliage Weeping River Wattle)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in well-drained to moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; Lime Magic is a compact, mounding river wattle selection grown for its bright chartreuse-lime cascading foliage rather than its flowers.

directions: Lime Magic is a compact river wattle selection bred for its dense, cascading mound of very fine, needle-like, bright chartreuse-lime foliage that holds its glowing color through the growing season, brightest in full sun and slightly softer green in more shade. Its lower, more mounded habit than the straight species makes it useful as a bold foliage accent, low hedge, or container specimen where a smaller-scale version of the weeping, fountain-like Acacia cognata texture is wanted. Small, pale yellow, fragrant pompom flowers appear in spring but are secondary to the foliage display. Grow in well-drained to moist, moderately fertile soil in full sun to part shade, and shear lightly after any winter cold damage to encourage dense new growth; it is more tolerant of damp soils than most acacias but still needs good drainage to avoid root rot.
sources: Australian native plant nursery cultivar notes
general horticultural reference on Acacia cognata cultivars
